question.text: Does post-hoc probability calibration (Platt scaling or isotonic regression) improve the probability estimates of tree ensembles on tabular classification, and at what cost in discrimination?

data.claim: Probability calibration trees outperform both isotonic regression and Platt scaling in reducing root mean squared error, indicating better calibration performance.
data.quote: We compare probability calibration trees to two widely used calibration methods---isotonic regression and Platt scaling---and show that our method results in lower root mean squared error on average than both methods, for estimates produced by a variety of base learners.

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration (via isotonic regression) improves model performance on Brier Score Loss, indicating better probability reliability for non-parametric models like Random Forest.
data.quote: Using re-calibration, the non-parametric models are able to outperform the Logistic Regression on Brier Score Loss.

data.quote: post-hoc calibration (Platt Scaling, Isotonic Regression) substantially improved probability reliability without sacrificing discrimination.

citation.title: Mitigating Algorithmic Bias Through Probability Calibration: A Case Study on Lead Generation Data

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration techniques such as Platt scaling and isotonic regression can reduce bias related to sensitive attributes like country of origin, without negatively affecting overall classification performance.
data.quote: The findings suggest that post hoc calibration can effectively reduce the influence of sensitive features on predictions by improving fairness without compromising overall classification performance.

citation.title: Calibration, Uncertainty Communication, and Deployment Readiness in CKD Risk Prediction: A Framework Evaluation Study

data.claim: Isotonic regression improves calibration, as measured by Expected Calibration Error (ECE), in CKD risk prediction models on internal data.
data.quote: Isotonic recalibration reduced internal ECE to 0.000-0.022.

data.claim: For Random Forests, isotonic regression may not significantly improve calibration unless applied with extensive calibration data, which may be impractical in data-scarce settings.
data.quote: The existing literature suggests that traditional calibration methods, such as isotonic regression, do not substantially enhance the calibration of RF probability estimates unless supplied with extensive calibration datasets.

data.claim: Platt scaling and isotonic regression were applied to improve the reliability of probability estimates in a tabular classification task.
data.quote: Probability calibration was applied using Platt Scaling and Isotonic Regression to improve reliability.

citation.title: ForeCal: Random Forest-based Calibration for DNNs

data.claim: A Random Forest-based calibration method (ForeCal) achieves better calibration (lower ECE) than existing methods with minimal loss in discriminative ability (AUC), indicating that post-hoc calibration can improve reliability without sacrificing discrimination.
data.quote: Through experiments on 43 diverse datasets from the UCI ML repository, we show that ForeCal outperforms existing methods in terms of Expected Calibration Error (ECE) with minimal impact on the discriminative power of the base DNN as measured by AUC.

citation.title: The crucial role of machine learning models in predicting current childhood asthma: model comparison, calibration, and SHAP-based interpretation

data.claim: Isotonic regression improves calibration of random forest probability estimates, while Platt scaling tends to worsen calibration, even though AUC (a measure of discrimination) remains stable.
data.quote: On the independent test set, calibration (10-bin reliability curves; Brier/ECE/intercept–slope) improved most with isotonic regression, specifically for Random Forest (ECE 0.0158 to 0.0086; intercept −0.174 to −0.010), whereas Platt scaling often worsened calibration, with AUC remaining largely stable across models (AUC ≈ 0.92–0.95).

citation.title: An Explainable and Fair AI Tool for PCOS Risk Assessment: Calibration, Subgroup Equity, and Interactive Clinical Deployment

data.claim: Random forest models can be effectively calibrated using isotonic regression to achieve a good balance between calibration and interpretability, with a reasonable Brier score and ECE.
data.quote: A calibrated Random Forest achieved a high predictive accuracy of 90.8%. SHAP analysis identified follicle count, weight gain, and menstrual irregularity as the most influential features, which are consistent with the Rotterdam diagnostic criteria. Although the SVM with isotonic calibration achieved the lowest calibration error (ECE = 0.0541), the Random Forest model provided a better balance between calibration and interpretability (Brier = 0.0678, ECE = 0.0666).

citation.title: A Lightweight Calibration-Selection Policy After a Probe Fit for Selective Classification on OpenML Tabular Tasks

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration methods such as temperature scaling and Dirichlet calibration improve the mean negative log-likelihood (NLL), indicating better probability accuracy, but may degrade the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), suggesting potential harm to the model's ability to perform well in abstention-based decision making.
data.quote: Within this benchmark, both tested calibrators improve mean NLL relative to raw predictions on average, yet calibration can also worsen mean AURC, so better probability fit does not imply better abstention behavior.

citation.title: Toward trustworthy cyber defense: A cognitive intrusion detection system with explainability and probabilistic uncertainty calibration

data.claim: Applying Platt scaling to a Random Forest model improves probabilistic reliability, as evidenced by a 45% reduction in Expected Calibration Error, indicating better alignment between predicted and actual probabilities.
data.quote: A Random Forest classifier was optimized and calibrated using Platt scaling to improve probabilistic reliability, while explainability was achieved through global and local SHAP analyses. Uncertainty was quantified using a probabilistic entropy-based metric and evaluated for stability across random seeds. Simulations on the CICIDS2017 Friday-Phishing dataset demonstrated near-perfect predictive performance, achieving an average F1-score of 0.9999 ± 0.0001, AUC = 1.0, and a 45% reduction in Expected Calibration Error following calibration.

data.claim: The Random Forest model, when used in a calibrated setting, achieves strong performance in both classification accuracy and calibration, as measured by a low Brier score of 0.009.
data.quote: Among all proposed models, Random Forest had the best overall metrics, achieving 0.989 accuracy and 0.990 F1 for the attack class, and the best calibration with a Brier score of 0.009.

data.claim: The DA2-Net model, which includes Brier-based calibration regularization, achieves superior or competitive performance in multiple evaluation metrics, including Brier score and Expected Calibration Error (ECE), indicating strong probability calibration.
data.quote: DA2-Net achieves or shares the best result in all 16 AUC blocks, 13 of 16 AUPRC blocks, 10 of 16 ACC blocks, 11 of 16 Brier blocks, and 7 of 16 ECE blocks.

data.description: The evidence does not provide a consistent comparison of Platt scaling and isotonic regression across multiple tree ensemble models beyond Random Forest. While E10 and E11 mention Random Forest, and E13 and E14 reference Platt scaling on Random Forest, there is limited or no evidence on how these methods perform on other tree ensembles such as Gradient Boosting Machines (e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM) in tabular classification. This limits generalizability of findings to broader ensemble models.

The impact of post-hoc calibration on discrimination metrics—such as AUC or AURC—is tested only in specific contexts. For instance, E10 notes that AUC remains stable with Platt scaling, but E12 indicates that calibration may worsen AURC, suggesting a potential trade-off. However, this trade-off is not systematically evaluated across different datasets or model architectures, and no clear consensus emerges on whether calibration universally preserves or degrades discrimination.

There is no direct empirical comparison of calibration performance (e.g., ECE, Brier score) between Platt scaling and isotonic regression across different base learners and data distributions. While E1 claims calibration trees outperform both methods, and E6 and E10 show improvements with isotonic regression, the relative performance of Platt scaling versus isotonic regression on diverse tree ensembles under varying data conditions (e.g., imbalanced, sparse, high-dimensional) remains underexplored.

The evidence lacks investigation into the cost of calibration in terms of computational efficiency, training time, or generalization stability—particularly when applied as a post-hoc step in real-world deployment pipelines. While calibration improves reliability, its practical cost in terms of time or scalability on large tabular datasets is not addressed in any of the cited studies.

data.independent_variable: calibration method (isotonic regression vs. Platt scaling)
data.rationale: G1 highlights a lack of evaluation beyond Random Forest on other tree ensembles (e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM), and G3 notes no direct empirical comparison of ECE between methods across diverse models. Evidence E1, E6, and E10 show isotonic regression outperforms Platt scaling in reducing ECE on Random Forest and in CKD models, and E10 shows improved calibration with isotonic regression (ECE from 0.0158 to 0.0086). This supports testing ECE across broader ensemble models.
data.statement: Post-hoc calibration using isotonic regression improves calibration (as measured by Expected Calibration Error, ECE) more than Platt scaling across multiple tree ensemble models (including Gradient Boosting Machines like XGBoost and LightGBM) in tabular classification tasks.

data.dependent_variable: Area Under the Risk-Coverage Curve (AURC) or AUC
data.independent_variable: calibration method (isotonic regression vs. Platt scaling)
data.rationale: G2 identifies conflicting evidence—E10 reports AUC remains stable, E12 notes calibration may worsen AURC, and E4 claims no harm to discrimination. This inconsistency demands empirical testing. The statement directly addresses this ambiguity by hypothesizing no degradation in AURC/AUC, despite improved calibration, thus testing the trade-off between reliability and discrimination across datasets.
data.statement: Post-hoc calibration via isotonic regression or Platt scaling does not degrade discrimination (as measured by AURC or AUC) in tabular classification, even when calibration improves probability reliability.

data.rationale: The hypothesis focuses on comparing isotonic regression and Platt scaling for calibration performance (ECE) across tree ensemble models in tabular classification. To test this, we include a diverse set of datasets (both balanced and imbalanced) to ensure generalization. The control condition uses Platt scaling on gradient boosting (a representative tree ensemble), while the treatment conditions extend the comparison to other tree ensembles (random forest, LightGBM) with both calibration methods. This design directly addresses gaps G1 and G3 by evaluating ECE across multiple tree ensembles beyond Random Forest, and includes imbalanced data to reflect real-world scenarios. The paired Wilcoxon test is used to compare ECE between the two calibration methods, as it is non-parametric and suitable for small sample sizes or non-normal distributions. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness, and three random seeds ensure reproducibility and variance estimation. The inclusion of both balanced and imbalanced datasets (e.g., breast_cancer_imb10, digits_binary_imb10) evaluates calibration under different data distributions, improving the real-world relevance of the results.

The hypothesis focuses on whether post-hoc calibration (via Platt scaling or isotonic regression) degrades discrimination, as measured by AURC or AUC, in tabular classification. To isolate the effect of calibration methods while controlling for model and dataset variability, we use a consistent base model (gradient boosting) to ensure comparability. We select three balanced, publicly available datasets—breast_cancer, digits_binary, and wine_binary—representing diverse feature distributions and class balances. These exclude imbalanced variants (e.g., _imb10) to avoid introducing bias from class imbalance effects that could confound the calibration-discrimination trade-off. The control condition (gradient_boosting) represents the uncalibrated baseline, while the two treatment conditions apply Platt and isotonic calibration respectively. A paired Wilcoxon test is used to assess differences in AURC/AUC between control and each treatment, as it is appropriate for non-normal, paired data. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness and reduces variance. Seeds 123, 456, 789 are used to ensure reproducibility and to allow for multiple independent runs, increasing confidence in the results. This design directly tests the hypothesis's core claim: that calibration does not degrade discrimination, despite improving reliability.
